trans-unit.source: A Message from Internet Archive Founder,
trans-unit.target: Un message du fondateur d’Internet Archive,

trans-unit.source: For more than two and a half decades, we have collected, preserved, and shared our digital cultural artifacts. Thanks to the generosity of our patrons, the Internet Archive has grown from a small preservation project into a vast library that serves millions of people each year. Our work has impacted the lives of so many of our users who value free and open access to information.
trans-unit.target: Depuis plus de vingt-cinq ans, nous collectons, préservons et partageons notre patrimoine culturel numérique. Grâce à la générosité de nos mécènes, Internet Archive est passé d’un petit projet de préservation à une vaste bibliothèque qui sert des millions de personnes chaque année. Notre travail a changé la vie de nombreux utilisateurs attachés à un accès libre et gratuit à l’information.

trans-unit.source: From the beginning, it was important for the Internet Archive to be a nonprofit, because it was working for the people. Its motives had to be transparent; it had to last a long time. That's why we don't charge for access, sell user data, or run ads, even while we offer free resources to citizens everywhere. We rely on the generosity of individuals like you to pay for servers, staff, and preservation projects.
trans-unit.target: Dès le départ, il était essentiel qu’Internet Archive soit à but non lucratif, car il œuvrait pour le public. Ses motivations devaient être transparentes, et il devait durer longtemps. C’est pourquoi nous ne faisons pas payer l’accès, ne vendons pas les données des utilisateurs et n’affichons pas de publicité, tout en offrant des ressources gratuites aux citoyens du monde entier. Nous comptons sur la générosité de personnes comme vous pour financer les serveurs, le personnel et les projets de préservation.

trans-unit.source: If you can't imagine a future without the Internet Archive, please consider supporting our work. We promise to put your donation to good use as we continue to build a long-term digital library.
trans-unit.target: Si vous ne pouvez pas imaginer un avenir sans Internet Archive, pensez à soutenir notre travail. Nous nous engageons à faire bon usage de votre don pour continuer à bâtir une bibliothèque numérique durable.

trans-unit.source: If you find our site useful, please chip in! Your support will help us build the web we deserve.
trans-unit.target: Si notre site vous est utile, donnez un coup de pouce ! Votre soutien nous aidera à bâtir le web que nous méritons.
Merci de vous joindre à moi.

trans-unit.source: As a project of the Internet Archive—a nonprofit internet library dedicated to promoting Universal Access to All Knowledge—Open Library is working to make digital texts available to everyone, everywhere. And we’re growing faster than ever before. Since we first launched, we have digitized more than 4.6 million texts, and are adding another 3,500 every single day.
trans-unit.target: Projet d’Internet Archive, bibliothèque numérique à but non lucratif qui défend l’accès universel à toutes les connaissances, Open Library s’efforce de rendre les textes numériques accessibles à tous, partout dans le monde. Et nous grandissons plus vite que jamais. Depuis notre lancement, nous avons numérisé plus de 4,6 millions de textes, et nous en ajoutons 3 500 de plus chaque jour.

trans-unit.source: Our ultimate goal for Open Library is to make all the published works of humankind available to everyone in the world. While large in scope and ambition, this goal is within our grasp. Achieving it will require the participation of librarians, authors, technologists, policy makers, and—importantly—supporters like you.
trans-unit.target: Notre objectif ultime pour Open Library est de rendre toutes les œuvres publiées de l’humanité accessibles à tous dans le monde. Même s’il est vaste et ambitieux, cet objectif est à notre portée. Pour l’atteindre, nous aurons besoin de la participation de bibliothécaires, d’auteurs, de technologues, de décideurs politiques et, surtout, de soutiens comme vous.

trans-unit.source: Because we firmly believe that libraries should be free, we will never run ads, sell user data, or charge for access to our collection. Instead, we rely on the generosity of individuals like you to pay for servers, staff, and digitization costs.
trans-unit.target: Parce que nous croyons fermement que les bibliothèques doivent être gratuites, nous n’afficherons jamais de publicité, ne vendrons jamais les données des utilisateurs et ne ferons jamais payer l’accès à notre collection. Nous comptons plutôt sur la générosité de personnes comme vous pour financer les serveurs, le personnel et les coûts de numérisation.

trans-unit.source: If you enjoy wandering our virtual stacks, please consider supporting our work. A little goes a long way, but fewer than 1 in 1,000 of our patrons donate. If you can afford to help, your support will help us build the library we deserve.
trans-unit.target: Si vous aimez flâner dans nos rayons virtuels, pensez à soutenir notre travail. Un petit geste compte beaucoup, mais moins d’un lecteur sur 1 000 fait un don. Si vous en avez les moyens, votre soutien nous aidera à bâtir la bibliothèque que nous méritons.

trans-unit.source: As a project of the Internet Archive—a nonprofit internet library dedicated to promoting Universal Access to All Knowledge—the Wayback Machine is continually working to ensure that the web has a memory. Our work has had powerful outcomes: We’ve been instrumental in helping journalists and fact-checkers hold those in power accountable. We’ve made it possible for individuals to access their digital memories. We’ve brought dead links back to life. Now, anyone with a reason to visit the internet of the past can easily access our growing collection at no cost.
trans-unit.target: Projet d’Internet Archive, bibliothèque numérique à but non lucratif qui défend l’accès universel à toutes les connaissances, la Wayback Machine œuvre sans relâche pour que le web ait une mémoire. Notre travail a eu des effets importants : nous avons aidé des journalistes et des vérificateurs de faits à demander des comptes aux puissants. Nous avons permis à chacun de retrouver ses souvenirs numériques. Nous avons redonné vie à des liens morts. Désormais, toute personne qui a une raison de visiter l’internet du passé peut facilement accéder gratuitement à notre collection en constante croissance.

trans-unit.source: Because we remain dedicated to promoting free access to information, we will never run ads, sell user data, or charge for access to the Wayback Machine. Instead, we rely on the generosity of individuals like you to pay for servers, staff, and maintenance.
trans-unit.target: Parce que nous restons attachés à la libre circulation de l’information, nous n’afficherons jamais de publicité, ne vendrons jamais les données des utilisateurs et ne ferons jamais payer l’accès à la Wayback Machine. Nous comptons plutôt sur la générosité de personnes comme vous pour financer les serveurs, le personnel et la maintenance.

trans-unit.source: If you can’t imagine a future without the Wayback Machine, please consider supporting our work. We promise to put your donation to good use as we continue to store more than 625 billion web pages, add over 585 million pages every day, and serve more than 600,000 Patrons every day. A little goes a long way, but fewer than 1 in 1,000 of our patrons donate. Your support will help us build the web we deserve.
trans-unit.target: Si vous ne pouvez pas imaginer un avenir sans la Wayback Machine, pensez à soutenir notre travail. Nous nous engageons à faire bon usage de votre don pour continuer à stocker plus de 625 milliards de pages web, à en ajouter plus de 585 millions chaque jour et à servir plus de 600 000 utilisateurs chaque jour. Un petit geste compte beaucoup, mais moins d’un utilisateur sur 1 000 fait un don. Votre soutien nous aidera à bâtir le web que nous méritons.

Reel-to-Reel and the First Online Fan Communities

In the 1960s, the Bay Area counterculture and the emerging tech world were in the same physical space. The Dead came into being in Palo Alto, California (in proto Silicon Valley) in the mid-1960s, a few miles down the road from Stanford University and the leading computer scientists of the age. Many of them, it turns out, loved Dead shows.
Owsley Stanley begins recording the soundboard of every live show, which is the first systematic documentation of a live rock band’s shows.
Betty Cantor-Jackson starts direct two-track reel-to-reel recordings of the live mix off the soundboards of Dead shows. Almost no one outside the band knows the recordings exist.

Deadheads are smuggling reel-to-reel recorders and mic stands into shows, under large coats, and at times pretending they were on crutches to slip by security. There were no formal rules against it, and enforcement was on a whim. The band’s position on it is inconsistent. This is the first fan-initiated live music audio documentation for any band.

Tapes begin to get circulated, and dubbed. Quality degrades with each generation of dub. Setlists are being maintained in typed notebooks and photocopied, and transmitted by postal mail. No computers.
First organized fan music trading network
Les Kippel ("Mr. Tapes") sets up a non-commercial tape trading network using postal mail. People in 48 states and abroad. Totally fan generated. The record labels had nothing to do with it.

The Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory has DEC PDP-10 mainframe computers on a time-sharing system called WAITS, and is the first institution in history where every researcher had a video terminal at their desk, like a phone. The researchers have a number of Deadheads among them, and keep a shared document on the system, one of the very first shared digital documents, their memory of Dead lyrics from the shows they were going to. The first crowdsourced digital lyrics database.

Previously you would have had to "go to the computer" to use it, and there was no such thing as "casual use" of a computer, rare multi-million-dollar machines with tightly rationed access. The team eventually gives a printout of the lyrics to the band, who didn’t have it all written down anywhere.
Among the earliest non-technical uses of government lab computers

The man who coined the term "artificial intelligence," John McCarthy, Turing Award winner and founder of the Laboratory, uses the WAITS system to post a ranked list of his favorite live versions of the song "St. Stephen," internal to the lab, before any of the research institutions were connected to the ARPANET. In 1972, Ned Lagin, at MIT making electronic music and a collaborator with the band, is given an account on the WAITS system (now connected to the ARPANET).
dead@SU-AI: the first online fan community

Paul Martin starts the first non-technical interest community on any computer network in history: an email list for people at the Laboratory and connected ARPANET nodes, registered in the static HOSTS.TXT file downloaded by every node on the network. Not just the first music community. The first computer-mediated fan community of any kind, for anything.

The same year, the first recorded act of online commerce is traced to the Deadhead community at Stanford and MIT: Deadhead hackers at the Stanford lab sell marijuana to Deadhead hackers at the MIT AI Lab over ARPANET. ARPANET is used to arrange the transaction; the physical handoff happens in person. In 1974, Phil Lesh visits the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory.
September 1974: the first dedicated print infrastructure for a music fan trading community. The classified "Want Page" for tape traders is the main draw.

Cassette supersedes reel-to-reel for fan trading. Dual-deck players make home copying trivial. The tape trading community explodes into hundreds of active traders maintaining elaborate postal correspondence systems, typed catalogs, and trade lists.

The generation system governs quality and status: Gen 1 (direct copy from master) is gold; Gen 4 is muddy. Access to low-generation tapes is social currency. The Dead’s music is travelling through a decentralised peer-to-peer network of humans with cassette decks and stamped envelopes, a human-powered BitTorrent.

An interviewer asks Garcia about "unauthorized recordings." Garcia is initially hostile, then realises the interviewer means fan trading, not commercial bootlegging. His position shifts. By 1982 he says: "When we are done with it, they can have it." This is the philosophical foundation on which everything downstream on the LMA is built.

A parallel community grows at MIT’s AI Lab, mirroring the Stanford scene. An East Coast Deadhead email list emerges at MIT. A fellow known as "Gumby" is going between Stanford and MIT, and the two communities are now linked across ARPANET, discussing shows, arranging tape trades, and doing whatever else Deadhead researchers did on government computers in the late 1970s.

Created by graduating researchers locked out of ARPANET. When you graduate from the universities and no longer have access to the lab computers and the network, what do you do? Build a new way to jack into the network, using phone lines and autodialers. Extremely slow, it could take a week to bounce a message from the US to Australia, but unstoppable.

Late 1981: net.music launches on Usenet, the first music newsgroup on any public network. In spring 1982, net.gdead forks from net.music, largely because the Dead-specific traffic was too large. This is the first band-specific dedicated discussion group on the public internet. (The Beatles get their own newsgroup in 1987.)
First digital live concert recording in America
April 1982: on PCM-Betamax digital tape, at a Dead show, by their soundman Dan Healy. A year before CDs become standard in the US.

October 27, 1984: the first officially sanctioned concert taping policy with a dedicated physical space. Dan Healy is complaining that the mic stands are blocking his view. The ticketing manager notices that there are 100–200 seats behind the board that never sell anyway because you can’t see the stage. The taping section is born; the band formalizes the policy that year.
The band understands that the taper network is the Dead’s unpaid, fanatically dedicated marketing department. The recordings are advertising for the shows.
The Grateful Dead conference on the WELL

February 1985: the WELL online community launches in Sausalito. On March 1, 1986, the Grateful Dead conference opens on the WELL, the first major online community for any musical artist. David Gans, John Perry Barlow, and much of the core intellectual Deadhead world are online.

The WELL Dead conference becomes the most vibrant online fan community of the pre-web era, pioneering norms of digital discourse, real identity ("You own your own words"), accountability, sustained long-form discussion, that shape the shape of the internet.
Usenet Grows Up, the EFF, and the Bandwidth Wall
By 1986 Usenet has grown unmanageable, and the Deadhead community’s two decades of experience with free information and decentralised community starts shaping the institutions of the internet itself.

Usenet is reorganised by the Backbone Cabal, the administrators of the largest, always-on backbone nodes, the people through whose machines most of Usenet’s traffic flows. net.gdead’s five-year legacy and large established community make its survival non-negotiable. It becomes rec.music.gdead.

rec.music.gdead is in the founding cohort of the rec.music.* hierarchy, one of only a handful of groups that arrive with an established community already behind them. It eventually reaches 38,000 readers and 9,000+ posts per month, one of the most active newsgroups anywhere on Usenet.
Barlow co-founds the Electronic Frontier Foundation

With Mitchell Kapor and John Gilmore, Grateful Dead lyricist John Perry Barlow founds the EFF to defend digital rights before most of the public understands what digital rights are. The founding philosophy flows directly from Deadhead culture’s two decades of experience with free information and decentralised community.

EFF board member Brewster Kahle, who will later found the Internet Archive, and board member John Gilmore, who co-created the alt.* Usenet hierarchy, both sit at the same table as Barlow. These three board relationships are the personal infrastructure that will, twelve years later, enable the Grateful Dead Archive at archive.org. The Dead community didn’t just build the internet. They built the organisations that protected it.
March 1994: Barlow publishes "The Economy of Ideas" in Wired, using the Dead as proof of concept for his ideas about the nature of copyright in the information economy.

This essay is the intellectual ancestor of Creative Commons licensing, open-source software philosophy, Spotify’s streaming model, and every information economy built on the principle that free distribution increases rather than decreases value.
The bandwidth wall: audio trading stays physical

A 90-minute concert at CD quality is approximately 800MB–1GB. On a university T1 line, a compressed show downloads in ~35 minutes; on a 28.8k modem, approximately 31 hours; on a typical 14.4k modem, approximately 62 hours. The internet can carry text, setlists, tape lists, trade requests, show reviews, and FAQs. It cannot carry audio.

The tape trading network remains entirely physical, cassettes and DATs organised by post, coordinated by digital networks but delivered by the postal service. The internet is the card catalogue. The tapes are still in the mail.
gdead.berkeley.edu: the first persistent digital archive

A UC Berkeley server becomes the central repository for Grateful Dead digital assets: typed setlists from 1972 onward, show statistics, tape label templates, guitar tablature, FAQs, lyrics, and images. Accessed via anonymous FTP, text-only, command-line, Unix knowledge required. The setlist database, built by Jerry Stratton and others, is the first systematically organised, collaboratively maintained digital record of any artist’s live performances.
The FAQ walked novice users through FTP protocol step by step, because the community understood that new people needed to be brought in. Deadheads were not gatekeepers. They were onboarders.
The Web Arrives, DAT Democratises Quality, Jerry Dies
The Dead have a web presence before most bands know the web exists, because the people who built the web and the people who followed the Dead were, to a remarkable degree, the same people.
Mosaic, and the Dead’s first web presence

Mark Leone at CMU builds one of the first Grateful Dead web pages, linking to the gdead.berkeley.edu FTP archive. In 1994, dead.net launches, the first official band website for a major rock band. And in 1992–93, the dead-flames mailing list at the University of Virginia is formally two-way gatewayed to rec.music.gdead: post to either system, appear in both.
DAT supersedes cassette for serious tapers

The first perfect-copy tape format, the end of generational degradation. The social structure of taping culture, built around scarcity of quality, is democratised. The music is ready for the digital age. The network is not yet fast enough to carry it.
Lossless Files, etree, and the Pre-Archive Era
Lossless compression finally makes audio tradeable, and the community builds the cataloging system that will become the metadata backbone of the Live Music Archive.

The Shorten codec compresses lossless audio to ~50–60% of WAV file size. A concert drops from ~800MB to ~400–500MB. Simultaneously, internet speeds rise, university connections hit 10Mbps; early broadband reaches 1–2Mbps for consumers. A show can now download in a few hours on a fast connection.

Deadheads begin distributing .SHN files through Usenet binary groups (alt.binaries.gdead) and individual volunteer FTP servers. It works, but barely, no central index, no quality verification, no standardised metadata, no way to know if what you’re downloading is what it claims to be.

Summer 1998: Steve Hormell founds etree.org, the first organised digital lossless music trading community, around three principles: "Live, Lossless, Legal." It allows only taper-friendly artists, no commercial releases, no profiteering. Within four years: 12,000+ users, 300 volunteer FTP servers.

The SHNID (Shorten ID) system assigns a unique identifier to every known circulating show, tracking source, lineage, encoding parameters, and community quality ratings. This cataloging system, built by volunteers, becomes the metadata backbone of the eventual Internet Archive collection as the Live Music Archive. etree is the bridge, the moment the physical tape economy fully becomes a digital file economy.
The Grateful Dead Internet Archive Project

The first systematic effort to digitise and catalogue a complete concert archive for any artist. A group of volunteers begins the systematic collection and conversion of Grateful Dead recordings into lossless format. Tom Anderson creates db.etree.org, assigning MD5 hashes to every circulating show, a cryptographic fingerprint that lets anyone verify an exact copy.
The goal: a complete, quality-verified catalogue of every circulating Dead recording, organised with the obsessive completist attention that only a community of Deadheads could sustain.
Unlimited storage. Unlimited bandwidth. Free. Forever. The community’s response: "We don’t believe you. But if you could, that would be our dream."
Jon Aizen proposes the Live Music Archive
July 23, 2002: Internet Archive engineer and Deadhead Jon Aizen posts to the etree mailing lists: the Archive will host etree-approved shows. Unlimited storage. Unlimited bandwidth. Free. Forever.

August 12, 2002: Aizen uploads a Rusted Root audience recording, the first free, unlimited, permanent streaming archive for live music. Within weeks etree members begin uploading in volume. The Grateful Dead permission comes through Brewster Kahle’s EFF board connection to John Perry Barlow.
The Grateful Dead Archive goes live on archive.org

Every circulating audience recording of every known show, thousands of concerts spanning 1965–1995, freely streamable and downloadable by anyone on earth. No login. No fee. No restriction. The endpoint of a 35-year journey from Owsley’s reels at the Fillmore to Cornell 5/8/77 on your phone, from a typed setlist in a manila folder to a searchable database of 8,000 shows.

November 2005: Grateful Dead Productions removes download access to all soundboard recordings, restricting them to streaming-only. The community erupts. The compromise holds to this day: audience tapes trade freely, soundboards stream for all, and the archive keeps growing, one lineage-documented tape at a time.

This culture is not just some thing of the past, it is still quite happening. Tonight you can be sure that somewhere tapers have mic trees up. They are recording which gear they are using, or noting the sources and generations of old recordings they’ve come across, exactly as their predecessors did with index cards. Its the same community, on the vanguard of the technology of the day, as always. Fresh recordings arrive at the LMA every single day, lineage documented, checksummed, and free for humanity to enjoy.

An ode to the tapers, archivists, and community maintainers of the Live Music Archive

The Live Music Archive at the Internet Archive is the result of over half a century of the co-evolution of live music, recording mediums, computers, and the Internet. It is the next logical step in a string of firsts in the history of networked computing, digital community, and the free flow of information online.

The LMA is fueled not only by the bands who play, and kindly permit the non-commercial recording of their shows, but also a by truly unique community of tapers and archivists which continues to thrive and grow today. This collection is the result of this collaboration between bands and their fans; and populated and maintained by volunteers. We thank them each and all.
Listening to the LMA is stepping into a cultural lineage which has in every era been on the vanguard of the technology of the day. It’s deep, and it will all make sense to you shortly.

In telling the story of the Live Music Archive, it would be impossible, and even ineffective, to separate its existence from the band called the Grateful Dead. This story is no comment on whether you should like their music (some really do, some really don’t), yet understanding their particular fans and culture help us to understand more clearly how this all came to be.

That is… how you landed at a vast freely accessible digital music archive, on a modern player, streamed real time, across the internet, in high fidelity, on a highly portable or semi portable computer, with full precise metadata, provenance chain, songlists, notes, and comments. And all of it possibly sourced from a notebook and reel-to-reel recorder that was smuggled into a show in 1968.
Timeline of live show recording culture

Remember, these are not ‘bootlegs’, they are permitted non-commercial recordings, generously curated and provided by lovers of music, which reminding us listeners, with every stream, why we’re going to buy a ticket to that next live music show that comes through town …or we’ll go on a road trip to see them. (Note: “Road trip mode” is the little truck icon on the mobile player :). Enjoy!
Compiled and told by Alden Bevington, Barlow's Knights Apprentice, friend of the aforementioned band, and designer for the Internet Archive. Contact him with any comments, or to correct the record :)

The music-loving archivists who built and continue to build this collection record not only the shows, but the provenance and lineage of every recording, and with a rigor most institutions would envy.

At the Live Music Archive you can simply enjoy the tunes and think no more, or go deep into the history of every generation from the original source, medium transfer, mic used, and mix applied. If you decide to go in deeper, it adds something like an EQ slider of “culture” that makes it all feel even richer.
This section is provided as an entry point into the culture that feeds the LMA… an overview of what’s going on here, from a taper’s eye view.

Every tape travels with its records: an info file naming the gear, the taper, the transfer chain; md5 and ffp fingerprints proving no bit changed hands; a shnid catalog number in the community database. Setlists are verified against decades of collective record-keeping , down to which songs segued and what Jerry said before the encore.
Recorded by the crew, taped by the fans, kept by everyone, thank the taper next time a 1977 soundboard hits your headphones.
